chief_complaint: hypertension in arms and weak femoral pulses
hpi_details: A 59-year-old male presents with hypertension in the arms and weak femoral pulses, raising concern for previously undiagnosed coarctation. Symptoms have become progressively more concerning.
ideas: He thinks his arteries are severely clogged with cholesterol, blocking normal blood flow down into his legs.
concerns: He is worried that the extreme pressure in his upper body will trigger a sudden, disabling stroke.
expectations: He hopes to get an imaging scan of his blood vessels and a stronger prescription to get his blood pressure under control.

investigation_events.title: CT angiography of the aorta
investigation_events.availability_message: The aortic CT angiography report is now available.

results.value: Severe focal coarctation just distal to the left subclavian artery with minimum lumen 4 mm and extensive intercostal collateral vessels

clinical_knowledge.topic: Coarctation of the Aorta evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Coarctation of the Aorta is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Plan for Coarctation of the Aorta: Echocardiogram, chest CTA, refer for surgical resection or stenting, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Coarctation of the Aorta.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Essential hypertension without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Very high blood pressure with headache or chest pain — needs prompt evaluation.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A congenital narrowing of the descending thoracic aorta causing high blood pressure in the arms but weak, delayed pulses in the legs — often first noticed in young patients on routine exam.
differentials: Peripheral arterial disease (common cause of diminished femoral pulses at this age; must be distinguished from coarctation)
red_flags: Very high blood pressure with headache or chest pain — needs prompt evaluation

must_ask.say: How was this discovered — during a routine check-up?
Have you noticed weakness or cramping in your legs with exercise?
Does anyone in your family have heart problems?
When was your blood pressure first noted to be high?

history.answer: I came in because I was told during a routine health checkup that my blood pressure in my arms was very high, and the doctor advised me to get evaluated.
At the clinic last week, the nurse checked both arms twice and said it was around 170 over 95, which is the first time anyone told me it was that high.
I bought an arm cuff monitor to check at home over the last few days, and it has consistently stayed between 165 and 175 systolic.
I was resting quietly for ten minutes beforehand, had not had any coffee, and was not in pain or rushing.
I have noticed a dull, throbbing ache at the back of my head over the past few weeks, but no sudden thunderclap pain or vision trouble.
No, I have not had any tearing chest or back pain, and I do not feel breathless at rest.
When I walk for about ten to fifteen minutes, both of my legs feel heavy, tired, and achy, so I have to stop and rest before continuing.
I have no difficulty breathing when lying flat, and my ankles or feet have never swollen up.
My urination is completely normal, with no blood, foamy urine, or waking up at night to urinate.
I have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure before, and I have never taken any blood pressure medications.
No, I do not get sudden spells of a pounding heart, profuse cold sweats, or turning pale.
I have not noticed generalized muscle weakness or frequent muscle cramps, just the tired feeling in my legs when walking.
My weight has remained steady, I do not bruise easily, and I handle hot and cold temperatures normally.
My wife says I do not snore heavily or stop breathing in my sleep, and I wake up feeling well rested.
I have never had kidney disease, recurrent urinary tract infections, or abnormal kidney function tests.
I do not take pain relievers, steroids, herbal medications, nasal decongestants, or diet pills.
I do not have diabetes, high cholesterol, or any prior history of a heart attack or stroke.
I eat regular home-cooked meals, avoid overly salty broths or processed food, and do not add extra salt.
I try to take regular walks, but recently my legs become fatigued and sore more quickly so I have had to shorten them.
My father developed high blood pressure in his sixties, but no one in my family had early heart attacks, strokes, or kidney failure.
I have always been in good health and have no chronic medical conditions.
I have never had surgery and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I have no known allergies to medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink socially, having one or two beers once or twice a month at most.
I work as an office manager and live with my wife in an apartment.

I figured all the blood is getting stuck in my upper body because my arteries down into my legs are severely clogged with plaque. I'm really worried that having such high pressure in my head and arms is going to cause a massive stroke.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 172/96 mmHg in the right arm and 170/94 mmHg in the left arm, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, and body temperature is 36.8°C.
Mild retinal arteriolar narrowing without hemorrhages, exudates, or papilledema.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, non-tender, and without palpable nodules or bruits.
Jugular venous pressure is normal at 2 cm above the sternal angle without abnormal distension.
Symmetric chest expansion without deformities; faint continuous pulsations are palpable along the posterior intercostal spaces.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields without wheezing, rales, or rhonchi.
Normal S1 and S2 with a grade 3/6 late systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border and radiating distinctly to the interscapular back.
Normal bowel sounds present; no renal artery or abdominal aortic bruits heard.
Soft, flat, and non-tender throughout with no hepatosplenomegaly or pulsatile abdominal mass.

Radial pulses are full and bounding bilaterally, whereas femoral, popliteal, and pedal pulses are markedly diminished and delayed bilaterally with noticeable radio-femoral delay; lower extremities feel mildly cool.
No pitting edema over the pretibial areas or ankles bilaterally.
No moon facies, buffalo hump, purple abdominal striae, or abnormal cutaneous bruising.
